target_segments.source_text: Then a crosswind slammed into him, hard enough to tear one of his signal streamers clean off its ring, and the glider skidded sideways toward the corridor's edge.
They reached the island together, with less margin than either had planned for.
"Ten minutes, and we watch the light in the corridor; we want to be out before it fades.
Across the bridge, he reached a cliff edge and could look out over the whole interior, and what he saw stopped him cold: the old knots didn't stop.
Arda stood between the two of them—the gate and the unfinished sentence—and felt his whole body leaning toward the gate, the way the flattened trees leaned toward the wind.
They reached the bridge too late; its far anchors had already begun to tear loose.
The bridge sagged and could no longer carry them.

They came down through the mist-filled trees at a dead run and found the great root span torn loose in the wind, its far anchor ripped out, the whole thing sagging and thrashing above a drop into the cloud sea.
He got three-quarters across before the anchor trunk groaned.
The bridge was sinking, and the line from the trunk was still clipped to his harness.
There was only one thing left to do, and he hated every second of it: he unclipped the line from his harness and let the sinking bridge go.
The bridge fell away beneath him into the cloud sea, and Arda swung free on the line Nisa still held. She leaned out and hauled; his hand found her wrist, and her grip found him.
"My line," he said, looking at the loose end in his hand.
"Your line," Nisa agreed, "and it did its job."
Their gliders still lay where the old knotted trunk leaned, just as they'd left them, both of them safe.
They landed at Stormbreak Watch as the sun sank low, shaking, mud-caked, out of rope, and entirely, completely victorious.
